segments.narration: A two-story wave of warm molasses swallowed an entire city neighborhood. In 1919, a steel tank in Boston exploded, unleashing two million gallons of sludge.
The thirty-five-mile-per-hour wave crushed buildings and buckled elevated railway tracks. The company immediately blamed anarchist explosives.
But there was no bomb—it was fatal physics. Unseasonable warmth caused fermenting syrup to expand, building massive gas pressure inside.
Modern analysis proved the steel walls were half as thick as safety codes required and cracked easily in winter cold.
The owners had even painted the tank brown to hide visible leaks. If executives knew the structure was failing, why did they fill it?

accuracy_flags.claim: The Boston molasses flood destroyed buildings and knocked over elevated railway tracks.
accuracy_flags.note: It was the company (USIA) that blamed anarchists to escape liability, not government officials. Additionally, the reference states the tracks were buckled rather than snapped.

verdicts.claim: In January 1919, a steel storage tank in Boston exploded, unleashing over two million gallons of molasses in a wave up to 25 feet high.
verdicts.note: The reference confirms a 50-foot steel storage tank burst on January 15, 1919, releasing 2.3 million gallons of molasses in a wave reaching 25 feet high.

verdicts.claim: The Boston molasses flood destroyed buildings and knocked over elevated railway tracks.
verdicts.note: It was the company (USIA) that blamed anarchists to escape liability, not government officials. Additionally, the reference states the tracks were buckled rather than snapped.
verdicts.correction: The thirty-five-mile-per-hour wave crushed buildings and buckled elevated railway tracks. The company immediately blamed anarchist explosives.

verdicts.claim: A sudden rise in temperature caused gas from fermenting molasses to build pressure inside the sealed tank.
verdicts.note: The reference notes that rapidly rising temperatures assisted carbon dioxide gas production from fermentation, building internal pressure inside the tank.

verdicts.claim: Modern scientific tests showed the tank's steel walls were half as thick as required by safety standards.
verdicts.note: A 2014 investigation confirmed the steel was half as thick as safety standards required and lacked manganese, making it brittle in cold weather.

verdicts.claim: The tank's owner, United Industrial Alcohol, painted the structure brown to hide leaking molasses.
verdicts.note: The reference explicitly states that the tank leaked so badly when filled that it was painted brown to hide the leakage.
